title: dnstree trace
description: One resolution walked from the root servers down, as dnstree --format json writes it. schema_version is raised whenever a field changes meaning or goes away, never for one that is merely added, so no object here forbids properties it does not name: a reader that understands a version keeps understanding it. A field that carries nothing is left out rather than written empty, so absence is the ordinary case and not an error.

schema_version.description: The version of this document's shape. It is written as a single value rather than a lower bound, because this schema describes that one version: a document of a later version has had a field change meaning or go away, and is not a document this schema can be read against.

elapsed_ms.description: How long the whole walk took. A walk from the root keeps no cache and takes every step itself, so it is the slow way round by design; resolver.elapsed_ms is what it means anything against.

started.description: When the walk began, in RFC 3339. It is what dnssec.signatures is read against, so that a trace read back later says how long its signatures had left when it was made.

resolvers.description: The same question put to recursive servers, in the order the run named them. Several of them is the question asked from several places at once: two that answer differently are two views of one name, and which of them a client gets depends only on which resolver it uses. A server that could not be asked at all is left out rather than carried empty.

root.description: The zone the walk started from. It carries no query of its own: its children are the servers that were asked. Absent when nothing was walked.

warnings.description: What the resolver could not do, in the order it found out.

without.description: What --without told the walk to treat as down: nameserver names, addresses and prefixes, as they were given. The servers inside them were never asked: the walk shows them as not queried, with a note saying which of these left them out, and a check that would have asked one carries an error saying so. An answer the walk found is one the rest of the DNS gives without them.

caa.description: Who may issue certificates for the name (RFC 8659), present only where --caa asked. A certificate authority looks for a CAA set at the name, then at each name above it short of the root, and goes by the first it finds, following an alias for that one lookup. The steps that asked are in the tree, as asides.

asked.description: The names looked up, from the name up, until one decided or one failed.

owner.description: The name whose set decides. Absent where none was found, which leaves it to any authority.

records.description: The set that decides, one property each, its value as the zone wrote it.

issue.description: Who may issue for the name. Absent where any authority may; cas is empty where none may.

wildcard.description: Who may issue for a wildcard below the name: the issuewild properties where the set has any, and otherwise the same as issue.

refused.description: Why every authority has to refuse, whatever the set says: a lookup that failed in a zone with a chain of trust behind it, or a critical property nobody knows.

undecided.description: Why the climb could not say who may issue: a lookup that failed where no chain of trust was found behind the zone, which an authority may take as leave to issue, or a budget dnstree ran out of.

dnssec.description: The first verdict on the way up that is not secure, or else the one over the set that decided. A name with no set has to prove it, since dropping a set is all it takes to lift a restriction.

caa_lookup.description: One name a certificate authority asks on the way up.

found.description: none where the name has no set, set where it has one, failed where the lookup did not come back with an answer, which makes every authority refuse.

alias.description: The name the answer came from, where name is an alias.

caa_record.description: One property of the set that decides.

critical.description: The issuer critical flag: an authority that does not know the tag has to refuse.

known.description: Whether the tag is one whose meaning dnstree knows.

cas.description: The authorities, by the domain each identifies itself with.

question.description: What the resolution set out to answer.

resolver.description: The same question put to one recursive server. It is metadata: nothing about the walk depends on it, and a server that would not answer leaves error rather than failing the resolution.

error.description: Why the server could not be asked at all.

match.description: How its answer stands against the one the walk found, absent where there was nothing to compare. The two are allowed to differ honestly: a name tailored to where it is asked from will, since the walk and the resolver are rarely in the same place.

kept.description: What its TTL says of the copy it is serving, absent where it says nothing either way: longer, the walk's answer kept past the TTL the zone gives it; stale, an answer no server of the zone gave the walk, carrying the 30 seconds or less serve-stale hands out (RFC 8767). A reading, not a verdict.

discovery.description: What the resolver answered for _dns.resolver.arpa (RFC 9462), present only where --ddr asked. Nothing connected to what it offers, so no offer here is verified.

error.description: Why the question could not be asked at all.

designated.description: The encrypted resolvers it designates, in the order they arrived. Absent for a resolver that answered and designates none.
One encrypted resolver a plain one points at.

protocols.description: The transports its ALPN names, of dot, doh and doq. HTTP counts as doh only where a dohpath says where to send the queries.

port.description: Absent where each protocol's default port applies.

dohpath.description: The URI template a doh offer is reached at.

hints.description: The addresses the record says the target is at.

step.description: One query and the queries it led to.

zone.description: The zone the queried server is believed to serve.

kind.description: What the hop turned out to be. The values so far are zone (the synthetic node a trace starts from), referral, answer, cname, nodata (the name exists, the type does not), nxdomain, lame (not serving the zone it was asked about), filtered (an answer somebody decided rather than served, as the server's own extended error says), timeout, error and skipped (known, never queried). It is not written here as a closed set: a kind added later is an addition, and a reader should treat one it does not know as a hop it cannot interpret rather than as a broken document.

proto.description: What the query was carried over: udp, tcp, dot or doh.

start_ms.description: When the hop's first query went out, in milliseconds after started. The hop occupies start_ms to start_ms + rtt_ms, and hops that overlap were in flight together. Present on every hop that asked a server something, zero included, and absent throughout a walk saved before dnstree recorded it.

rtt_ms.description: What the whole hop cost, retries included. Absent where the hop took no measurable time.

size_bytes.description: The answer as it arrived, in bytes on the wire, which is what dig reports as MSG SIZE. Absent where nothing answered.

limit_bytes.description: The most that answer could have been without being truncated: the EDNS0 buffer the query advertised, or the 512 bytes a query carrying no EDNS0 is answered within. Absent over tcp, dot and doh, where a single answer is not bounded this way. A size_bytes near it is a server with no room left: one more record and every resolver asking pays a second round trip over TCP.

tight.description: Set where size_bytes leaves almost nothing of limit_bytes, meaning one more record in the zone truncates the answer. It is the reading of the two sizes, carried so that nothing reading a trace has to hold the margin itself.

records.description: What the server returned, where that is the point of the step.

notes.description: What it took to get the answer: a retry over TCP, a query sent again without EDNS0. They belong to this hop rather than to a new one.

nsid.description: What the server called itself, as RFC 5001 asks it to, absent where the query asked for no identifier or the server published none. It belongs to the answer rather than to the server: one anycast address is many machines, and this says which of them answered. An identifier whose bytes spell no printable name is carried as the hex it arrived as, and one longer than 32 bytes is cut and ends in an ellipsis.

cookie.description: How the server answered the DNS cookie the query carried (RFC 7873, --cookie), absent where the query carried none: without --cookie, over DoT and DoH, and on a query asked again without EDNS0. supported is our client cookie back with a server cookie of its own; absent is no cookie at all, which is allowed; mismatch is a client cookie other than the one sent, so the answer may not be the server's; malformed is a cookie of a length no cookie has; rejected is BADCOOKIE even to the server cookie the server handed out itself.

aside.description: Set on work that answers a different question: the address of a nameserver, or the NS set of a zone. The resolution's own answer is never inside one. Following an alias is not an aside: the target is what the question meant all along.

minimised.description: Set on a hop that asked for less of the name than the walk was after, to find where the next zone cut is (RFC 9156, --qmin). asked says what it put instead, and what it came back with is about that shorter name, so it is never the walk's answer.

children.description: The hops this one led to, in the order they were made.

name.description: The name the delegation gave it, absent where only the address is known.

port.description: Where the server was asked. A step of a finished trace always names it.

asn.description: The origin AS of a server address, looked up behind the walk. A prefix announced by more than one AS keeps the first of them. The lookups are best effort and never fail a resolution, so this is absent whenever they could not get through or ran out of time.

allocated.description: The date the prefix was handed out.

flags.description: The header bits worth showing on a hop. Only a bit that is set is written, so reading this is a question of presence: aa (authoritative answer), tc (truncated, the answer did not fit), ad (authenticated data), do (DNSSEC records were asked for) and edns (the server answered with EDNS0).

service.description: An HTTPS or SVCB record decoded. data carries every parameter as text; this is the part something reading the output can branch on.

ech.description: Whether the record publishes an encrypted client hello configuration. A client that finds one encrypts the name it is about to ask for, which is worth something only if the record reached it unforged.

asked.description: The question one hop put, which is not always the question the resolution set out to answer: a walk asks a zone for its keys, a parent for the DS of a cut, a zone for the NS set it holds of itself, each of its servers for the serial it is on, and the address of a nameserver named somewhere else. It is how a reader tells those apart from the hops the resolution itself is made of, without reading the notes a person reads. Absent on a hop that asked nothing: a server listed and never queried, or a note about why the walk stopped. The class is the document's own and is not repeated here.

soa.description: As much of a zone's start of authority as it is read for. It is present where the zone was asked for it outright, which --serial does of every nameserver, and on a nodata or an nxdomain, which carry the zone's SOA in place of the records they have none of.

serial.description: The version of the zone the answering server is serving. Two nameservers of one zone answering with different serials are answering out of different copies of it. Which of them is the newer is not something to work out by comparing the numbers: serial arithmetic wraps (RFC 1982).

ttl.description: The TTL on the SOA record itself, in seconds.

minimum.description: The last field of the SOA rdata, in seconds. A denial lives for the shorter of this and the TTL on the record (RFC 2308); both are carried, because which of them wins is a reading and this document records what the zone said.

delegation.description: The zone cut a referral pointed at.

ttl.description: How long the parent lets the referral be cached, in seconds. It is what a resolver goes on using these nameservers for after they have been changed, which is not the TTL on the answer below them and is usually a great deal longer.

zone_ttl.description: The TTL the zone gives its own NS set, in seconds, present only where --check-ns asked it. The two usually differ, since the parent's is often the registry's to choose, and a resolver that goes by the child's copy once it has one keeps the nameservers for this long instead.

ns.description: The nameserver names, in the order they were received.

glue.description: The addresses from the additional section that this zone was allowed to hand out, meaning the in-bailiwick ones. Bailiwick is judged against the zone the answering server serves, which is what lets the root hand out gTLD server addresses.

glueless.description: Nameservers inside the delegated zone that came with no glue. Nothing can resolve them, so the delegation is broken.

out_of_bailiwick.description: Nameservers named outside the delegated zone that came with no address the parent was entitled to give. They are found with a walk of their own instead.

ds_present.description: Whether the parent signed the delegation.

dnssec.description: How far the chain of trust got at one zone cut. A cut is judged from above, so this sits on the step that pointed at the zone rather than on the zone itself: on a referral it is the verdict of the zone in that referral's delegation.

state.description: secure is every link from the anchor down verified; insecure is a parent that proved it publishes no DS; bogus is a chain that breaks; indeterminate is a chain this build could not check, which is never the same as finding it broken.

zone.description: The zone the verdict is about, which is not always the zone of the step it sits on.

algorithm.description: The signing algorithm, so that an algorithm nothing here supports reads differently from a signature that genuinely does not verify.

signatures.description: The signatures a secure verdict rests on, as long as each was made to last: the keys of the zone, the DS its parent signed, the records that answered. Absent on any other verdict. A zone that stops being re-signed goes on validating until the first of them runs out, and then fails all at once.

keys.description: The zone keys of the zone's DNSKEY set, on a secure verdict about entering the zone. They say how it is set up rather than whether it validates.

ds.description: The DS records the parent signed for the zone, on a secure verdict about entering it, each held against the zone's keys. Absent for the root, whose DS are the trust anchors.

key.description: One zone key of a DNSKEY set.

sep.description: Flagged as a key signing key.

bits.description: The length of an RSA modulus. Absent for any other algorithm.

pointed.description: A DS of the parent digests to this key.

signs.description: A signature over the DNSKEY set names this key.

ds.description: One DS record a parent publishes for a zone.

digest.description: The digest type, such as SHA256.

match.description: matched where it digests one of the zone's keys, unmatched where it digests none, and unchecked where its digest type cannot be computed here, which says nothing either way.

probe.description: Set on the aside that asked a nameserver of the zone the walk ended in for what it should keep from strangers, with --check-axfr or --check-recursion. Nothing of what it gave is kept.

kind.description: transfer is the whole zone asked for by AXFR; recursion is a name outside its zones asked with recursion desired.

state.description: open where the server gave it, closed where it did not, and unchecked where it could not be asked, which says nothing either way.

dangling.description: Set on the hop that showed a name left pointing at something that is not there, which whoever creates that thing first can answer for. It says what the walk saw: a zone halfway through a move looks the same.

kind.description: nameserver: a nameserver whose name does not exist. alias: an alias whose target does not exist. lame: every nameserver of the zone answered without authority for it, which is how a hosting service answers for a zone nobody has created there.

name.description: What was left pointing: the zone delegated, or the alias.

target.description: What it points at: the nameserver, or the alias's target. Absent for lame.

missing.description: The name zone says does not exist: target or the ancestor of it directly below zone, and what somebody else would have to create there. Absent for lame.

zone.description: The zone whose denial says missing does not exist. Absent for lame.

nsec3.description: How the zone that denied something hashes its names (RFC 5155), read off an NSEC3 whose signature held. Absent where no NSEC3 was checked. RFC 9276 asks for no extra iterations and no salt.

zone.description: The zone that owns the NSEC3, which is the parent where it proved it publishes no DS.

iterations.description: The extra times each name is hashed.

salt.description: The salt, in hex. Absent for none.

signal.description: What the zone asks its parent to publish, in its CDS and CDNSKEY records (RFC 7344, RFC 8078), held against the DS the parent publishes. Present where --check-ds asked, on the verdict of the cut the DS belongs to.

state.description: none is a zone that proved it asks for nothing; match asks for the keys the parent holds; pending asks for another key than the parent holds, which is a rollover waiting on the parent; delete asks for no DS at all; inconsistent is a CDS and a CDNSKEY describing different keys, which a parent acts on neither of; unchecked is a request that could not be fetched, or was not signed by the zone's keys.

requested.description: The key tags the zone asks for.

held.description: The key tags the parent's DS names.

signature.description: How long one signature was made to last, in RFC 3339. One with less than a fifth of that left when the walk was made is late in its life, which is what a stopped signer leaves behind.

extended_error.description: What a server said about its own answer, in the codes of RFC 8914. An rcode says what happened; this says why, and it is the only thing in a reply that tells an answer withheld apart from an answer that is not there.

reason.description: The registered name of the code, absent for one this build does not know.

text.description: EXTRA-TEXT, whatever the server chose to add in words, whole. Every byte outside printable ASCII, and the backslash, is escaped as \DDD or \\.

withheld.description: Set where the code says somebody decided this answer rather than served it, so that a reader need not carry the list of which codes those are.

subnet.description: The client subnet of RFC 7871 as a server handed it back. A server that answers with one has taken it into account.

scope.description: How much of the prefix the server actually used. Zero is a server saying this answer is the same for everybody.
